title: Four lepers (2 Kings 7:3–9)
hook: outcasts find the enemy camp empty and decide to share the news

segments.voice: Yesterday, a servant's eyes were opened to a mountain full of chariots: more are with us. Today, Samaria is under siege and starving, and help comes from outside the gate.

Outside the gate of Samaria sit four men with a skin disease. The law keeps them outside the city, and the city is under siege by Aram, with famine inside. They do the math out loud: "Why sit we here until we die?" If we go into the city, there's famine, and we die there. If we sit here, we die here. So let's go over to the enemy camp. If they spare us, we live. If they kill us, we were dying anyway. At twilight, the four outcasts get up and walk toward the enemy.
screen: `FOUR MEN OUTSIDE THE GATE.` → `WHY SIT WE HERE UNTIL WE DIE?` → `WALKING TOWARD THE ENEMY.`

segments.voice: They reach the edge of the camp, and there's no one there. The Lord had made the army of Aram hear a noise of chariots and horses, the noise of a great host, and they fled in the twilight, leaving their tents, horses, donkeys, everything. So four hungry men walk into an empty camp full of food. They eat and drink in one tent, carry off silver, gold and clothing, and hide it. Then another tent. Who could blame them? And then they stop. One says: "We do not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace." These are the men the law kept outside the walls, and they're the ones who realize good news kept to yourself goes bad. They admit a plain worry, too: if we wait until morning light, some trouble will come upon us. So they go back in the dark and call to the gatekeepers: we came to the camp of Aram, and no one was there, only horses tied, and donkeys tied, and the tents as they were. The king suspects a trap. Scouts go out, find a trail of clothes and gear all the way to the Jordan. And the starving city walks out and eats. The good news came from the edge, from four people nobody expected to hear from. It reached the city because they decided a full stomach wasn't enough. A day of good tidings has to be told.
screen: `WHY SIT WE HERE UNTIL WE DIE?` · `AN EMPTY CAMP FULL OF FOOD.` · then, large: `WE DO NOT WELL.` · then: `GOOD NEWS FROM THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself what good thing you know that someone else doesn't: a job opening a friend could use, a thank-you you never passed on, praise you've said behind someone's back but never to their face. Let one come to mind, along with the person who needs it, and hold it ready, like the four men at the gate in the dark.
Four lepers. Outcasts at the gate of a starving city who found the enemy camp empty and decided they couldn't keep the news to themselves. Today's word.
Your line: a day of good tidings. The news came from outside the walls. That's day seven hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Jews read the story of the four lepers as a haftarah alongside the Torah's laws for healing from skin disease in Leviticus.

chat.says: The four lepers found food in the empty camp. Why didn't they just keep it?
options: They said we do not well: a day of good tidings had to be shared with the city.
The enemy came back for their tents, so they had to run to the city.
The king had ordered them to search the camp and report what they found.
chat.meaning: After eating and hiding loot, one said: we do not well, this is a day of good tidings and we hold our peace. So they told the gate.

Samaria.meaning: the besieged capital of Israel's northern kingdom

Aram.meaning: the kingdom whose army besieged the city

Jordan.meaning: the river the fleeing army ran toward

notes: Auditor (2026-10-01): practice opening varied; trapdoor floor now the Talmudic identification of the four as Gehazi and his sons (Sanhedrin 107b, Sotah 47a; paraphrase), Keeper verify folios.
Editor: removed 'nobody inside was sharing bread' (unfair to a starving city, not in the text) and 'food is gone inside and out'; varied the 'Think about' line; practice no longer says 'picture'.
Verify KJV wording at 2 Kings 7:3 and 7:9; JPS 1917 may be preferred.
'Four' is stated in 7:3 ('four leprous men') and kept because the text says it.
'The law keeps them outside the city' leans on Leviticus 13:46 (paraphrased).
The fleeing army (7:6–7), the report at the gate (7:10) and the scouts (7:12–15) are paraphrased and summarized.
'leper' follows KJV; tzara'at is a skin affliction, not necessarily modern leprosy.
